text: Siri (/ˈsɪri/ ⓘ SEER-ee) is a virtual assistant and chatbot developed and popularized by Apple Inc., included in iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, macOS, Apple TV, audioOS, and visionOS. It uses voice queries, gesture-based control, focus-tracking, and a natural-language interface to answer questions, make recommendations, and perform actions by delegating requests to Internet services. Over time, Siri adapts to users' individual language use, searches, and preferences, delivering personalized results. Originating from a project at the SRI International Artificial Intelligence Center, Siri is a spin-off of the DARPA-funded CALO project and was co-founded by Dag Kittlaus, Tom Gruber, and Adam Cheyer. The name Siri, a short form of the Old Norse name Sigrid (composed of "sigr" meaning victory and "fríðr" meaning beautiful), was named by Kittlaus after a co-worker in Norway. Siri's speech recognition engine was provided by Nuance Communications, which was acquired by Scansoft, later bought by Nuance; Apple licensed the recordings. The original American voice was recorded in July 2005 by Susan Bennett, unaware of its future use; a report in 2013 suggested Allison Dufty was the voice, but she denied it, and Bennett confirmed her role with audio forensics support. The original British male voice was provided by Jon Briggs, who narrated The Weakest Link and discovered his role in 2011; the original Australian voice was provided by Karen Jacobsen, known as the GPS girl. The initial prototype used the Active platform, a joint project between SRI International and École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, led by Didier Guzzoni, who became Siri’s chief scientist. Apple acquired Siri in April 2010 under Steve Jobs’ direction, and it was first released as a standalone app for iOS in February 2010, with plans for Android and BlackBerry devices. On October 4, 2011, Apple introduced Siri as a built-in feature of the iPhone 4S, removing the standalone app from the App Store. Third-party developers like Steven Troughton-Smith and "Chpwn" later ported and hacked Siri to run on older devices. Siri supports a wide range of commands, including phone actions, information checks, scheduling, device settings, Internet searches, navigation, entertainment queries, and interactions with iOS-integrated apps. With iOS 10 (2016), Apple opened limited third-party access via an API for messaging, payments, ride-sharing, and calling apps. iOS 11 added support for follow-up questions, language translation, and expanded third-party actions, including task management. In iOS 11, Apple also introduced typing to Siri and implemented on-device learning to improve suggestions. iOS 17 and iPadOS 17 enabled users to activate Siri by saying "Siri," while "Hey Siri" remains supported. In 2024, Apple introduced initial large language model (LLM) functionality to Siri in iOS 18, iPadOS 18, and macOS Sequoia, including ChatGPT integration, under the "Apple Intelligence" umbrella. In 2025, Apple announced a broader overhaul of Siri based on Apple Intelligence would be delayed due to technical challenges. In 2026, Apple selected Google Gemini to power AI features like Siri. Siri received mixed reviews upon its 2011 release, praised for voice recognition and contextual knowledge but criticized for stiff commands, lack of flexibility, poor understanding of accents, and limited information on nearby places. Critics noted Siri's lack of innovation compared to competitors like Amazon's Alexa, Microsoft's Cortana, and Google's Assistant, with concerns over voice recognition, service integrations, and Apple's prioritization of user privacy and internal power struggles. In 2017, a report highlighted Apple's slow progress in voice assistant innovation, citing privacy policies and internal conflicts. In 2019, a former Apple contractor revealed that Siri occasionally records user conversations when activated and sends them to contractors evaluating responses. Siri has also faced criticism from pro-abortion rights groups, including the ACLU and NARAL Pro-Choice America, for failing to provide information on birth control or abortion providers and instead directing users to crisis pregnancy centers. Apple stated these were not intentional omissions, and while Siri began offering more comprehensive lists of Planned Parenthood facilities, adoption clinics still appear near the bottom of results. Siri has also struggled with users having distinctive English accents, such as Scottish or Southern U.S. accents. In March 2012, Frank M. Fazio filed a class-action lawsuit claiming Apple misrepresented Siri’s capabilities, alleging the iPhone 4S was merely a more expensive iPhone 4. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2013 due to insufficient documentation of misrepresentation. In June 2016, The Verge reported that Siri's core flaws—poor voice recognition and clunky results—remained unresolved, especially as competitors advanced. In October 2016, Bloomberg reported Apple planned to unify its cloud services teams to improve Siri’s query processing, though The Verge later reiterated in 2017 that Siri's voice recognition remained "bad." Apple has expanded Siri to newer iPhone models, iPad, iPod Touch, Mac, AirPods, Apple TV, HomePod, and Apple Vision Pro. In 2021, Apple announced Siri integration for third-party devices on the same network as a HomePod or HomePod Mini, with the Ecobee SmartThermostat becoming the first such device in October 2021. In 2024, Denon added Siri control to select soundbars and smart speakers. Siri also offers humorous pre-programmed responses, such as "All evidence to date suggests it's chocolate" to "What is the meaning of life?" or "My End User Licensing Agreement does not cover marriage" to "Will you marry me?" Initially limited to female voices in most countries, Apple added a male voice option in June 2013, with notable exceptions in the UK, France, and the Netherlands. In September 2014, users could say "Hey Siri" to activate the assistant without holding the device, and in September 2015, individualized voice recognition was introduced to prevent unauthorized activation. In iOS 17 and iPadOS 17, Siri supports back-to-back requests and bilingual queries. In iOS 18, iPadOS 18, and macOS Sequoia, Siri features an updated interface, improved natural language processing, and text interaction via double-tapping the home bar (without enabling in Accessibility). Apple states Siri now uses device context to make conversations more natural, provides device support, and offers larger app support via the Siri App Intents API. For example, a user can ask, "When is Mom's flight landing?" and Siri will cross-reference flight details with real-time tracking. Siri also summarizes messages across apps like Discord and Slack, though users note this can be inappropriate in certain situations. Apple Intelligence enables Siri to deliver personalized, context-aware intelligence using on-device information. Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt acknowledged that Siri could threaten Google's core search business.

Siri's voice recognition has been described as "bad."[88] In June 2017, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was falling behind in voice assistant innovation due to competitors like Amazon and Google advancing in the field, noting that Apple workers' anxiety levels "went up a notch" upon learning of Amazon's Alexa. The report attributed this lag to Apple's emphasis on user privacy—such as storing randomly-tagged six-month Siri searches—compared to Google and Amazon, which retain data until users actively delete it,[clarification needed] and internal executive power struggles at Apple. Apple did not respond to the report, though Eddy Cue stated: "Apple often uses generic data rather than user data to train its systems and has the ability to improve Siri's performance for individual users with information kept on their iPhones."[15][89] In July 2019, an anonymous former Apple contractor, Thomas le Bonniec, revealed that Siri regularly records user conversations when activated, often unintentionally, and sends these recordings to Apple contractors who grade Siri's performance on various factors. These recordings include private doctor-patient conversations, business deals, and intimate moments between couples. Apple did not disclose this in its privacy documentation and provided no opt-in or opt-out option.[90] In August 2019, Apple apologized, suspended the Siri grading program, and stated it would resume "later this fall when software updates are released to [its] users."[91] The company also announced it would no longer listen to Siri recordings without user permission.[92] iOS 13.2, released in October 2019, introduced the ability for users to opt out of the grading program and delete all stored voice recordings on Apple's servers.[93] Users could choose whether their audio data was sent to Apple, with the ability to change their decision at any time, making the program opt-in. In May 2020, Thomas le Bonniec revealed himself as the whistleblower and sent a letter to European data protection regulators, urging them to investigate Apple's "past and present" use of Siri recordings, arguing that despite the apology, Apple has not faced consequences for its years-long grading program.[94][95] In December 2024, Apple agreed to a $95 million class-action settlement to compensate users of Siri-enabled devices from the past ten years and committed to confirming the deletion of Siri recordings before 2019 (when the feature became opt-in) and issuing new guidance on data collection and user participation in improving Siri.[96] Apple has developed various accessibility features to make its devices more inclusive for individuals with disabilities, allowing users to share feedback via email.[97] Features include live speech, personal voice, Siri's atypical speech pattern recognition, and more.[98] Siri, like many AI systems, can perpetuate gender and racial biases; The Conversation argued that Siri reinforces the role of women as secondary and submissive to men due to its default soft, female voice.[103] According to The Scientific American, Claudia Lloreda noted that non-native English speakers must "adapt our way of speaking to interact with speech-recognition technologies."[104] Due to repeated learning from a large user base, Siri may unintentionally reflect a Western perspective, limiting representation and reinforcing biases in interactions. Despite these issues, Siri offers significant benefits, especially for people with disabilities who face barriers in using technology and accessing the internet. Apple has since expanded Siri's voice options to include various accents and languages.[105] The iOS version of Siri includes a vulgar content filter, but it is disabled by default and must be enabled manually by the user.[106] In 2018, Ars Technica reported a glitch where requesting the definition of "mother" caused Siri to respond by saying "mother" is short for "motherfucker" when the user replies "yes"—a response derived from third-party sources like the Oxford English Dictionary, not from Apple.[107] This led to numerous YouTube videos showing the responses or how to trigger them. Apple silently fixed the issue. Siri also provided the voice of 'Puter in The Lego Batman Movie.[109]
